\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When synthetic text is recursively fed back as input, the resulting multi-generational content degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively prompting a fixed model to generate from its own prior outputs); we study prompt-chains, which isolate text-intrinsic information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically and ignores the generational depth dimension.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/pipeline.pdf}
\caption{Generational depth estimation pipeline. Seed documents are recursively passed through a generation operator $G_\delta$ to produce a depth chain. Statistical features are fed to the OBD-LightGBM classifier for depth prediction.}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure*}

This gap cuts across multiple communities.
Binary detectors~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate (Section~\ref{sec:binary_confidence}).
Membership inference~\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question, and the model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} provides no per-text tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} likewise ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone.

Knowing whether the discriminable depth is finite, and where it saturates, has direct practical consequences.
For data curation, the saturation point determines filtering granularity: if discrimination collapses at depth 2, graduated weighting beyond that boundary injects noise, and binary filtering becomes the principled choice.
Model collapse theory predicts monotonic quality degradation across generations, but existing analyses are population-level and provide no per-text measure of where degradation saturates.
$\Kempirical$ fills this gap by localizing the generation at which adjacent outputs become empirically indistinguishable.

The Data Processing Inequality implies that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$; its actual value is determined empirically.
We present an empirical characterization study that formalizes $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations) and measures it under prompt-chain generation using 15 statistical features computed via a fixed reference scorer (Section~\ref{sec:features}) and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.

\section{$\Kempirical$-Consistent Filtering}
\label{sec:filtering}

As a consistency check (not a standalone contribution), we test whether $\Kempirical{=}2$ predicts the correct filtering strategy.
We compare six strategies on 30{,}000 prompt-chain documents (depths 0--5, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct): no-filter, binary-ours, binary-Drayson~\citep{drayson2025}, graduated weighting, surprisal, and DSIR~\citep{xie2023dsir}.
Binary filtering reduces MMLU degradation from $-$1.53\,pp to $-$0.77\,pp ($p_{\text{corr}} < 0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:tab_filtering_main}): binary exploits the one reliable boundary (0v1), while graduated strategies inject noise by weighting depths 2--5 with near-random scores.
Cross-model replication confirms binary $>$ graduated across contamination ratios 10--50\% (Appendix~\ref{sec:pythia_filtering}, \ref{sec:dose_response}).
On arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$), graduated filtering similarly fails, so $\Kempirical$ measures discriminability but overestimates filtering utility (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
